title: Cooling and delocalizing thermal oscillators in hollow-core fibers using optical fringes
authors: Soumya Chakraborty, Pardeep Kumar, Gordon K. L. Wong, Claudiu Genes, Nicolas Y. Joly
abstract: Trapped particles in hollow-core fibers enable long-range sensing, though advanced control of their in-fiber motion, such as multimodal cooling and squeezing, remains challenging. Here, we present optical interference-based techniques for controlling a fringe-trapped silica nanoparticle inside a fiber. After feedback-cooling its axial and radial motion, we induce axial delocalization (position anti-squeezing) via two approaches. First, non-adiabatic fringe suppression expands position variance by 11.83 ($\pm$0.7) dB to that of the initial cold-state while retaining Gaussian statistics. Second, multi-pass particle positioning at dark fringes increases delocalization to 13.23 ($\pm$0.5) dB relative to the cold-state's variance via inverted potentials, in agreement with stochastic theory. Stronger delocalization produces non-Gaussian states. Our results demonstrate fringe-trapped particles in hollow-core fibers as a versatile platform for long-range sensing and macroscopic quantum physics.
summary: This research demonstrates advanced control over trapped nanoparticles in hollow-core fibers, achieving both deep cooling and controlled axial delocalization (anti-squeezing). By utilizing optical fringe manipulation, the authors quantify delocalization enhancements exceeding 13 dB, establishing the fiber as a versatile platform for macroscopic quantum physics and long-range sensing.
main_problem: The paper addresses the advanced control of in-fiber motion for trapped nanoparticles, specifically achieving multimodal cooling and inducing controlled axial delocalization (position anti-squeezing).
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated delocalization enhancements of up to 13.23 dB using multi-pass positioning at dark fringes, while also showing that strong delocalization leads to non-Gaussian quantum states.
method: The study employs optical interference techniques, combining phase-adaptive feedback cooling with pulsed manipulation of the trapping potential via polarization control or fringe shifting.
model_or_system: The physical system is a silica nanoparticle trapped within a hollow-core photonic crystal fiber (HC-PCF) using optical standing waves formed by interfering counterpropagating modes. The dynamics are modeled using the evolution of the covariance matrix in phase space.
key_observables: Position variance ($\Delta x^2$), delocalization enhancement (measured in dB relative to the cold state), and center-of-mass temperatures.
important_parameters: Cooling temperatures near 1 K, delocalization enhancements up to 13.23 dB, and the relative polarization angle ($	heta_p$) used for pulsing.
main_assumptions: The delocalized state is assumed to relax toward the initial thermal state under thermal noise, and the analysis relies on modeling the evolution of the covariance matrix through deterministic propagators and noise terms.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup for dual-beam trapping, show the cooling of eigenmodes, and depict the evolution of phase-space distributions, demonstrating the transition from squeezed to anti-squeezed states.
paper_structure: The paper details the cooling protocols, then presents two distinct delocalization protocols: non-adiabatic fringe suppression (Protocol A) and multi-pass positioning at dark fringes (Protocol B). It mathematically models the covariance evolution across these pulsed cycles, concluding with an analysis of recoil heating in dark vs. bright traps.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly controllable platform for studying quantum non-Gaussian dynamics and quantum non-linear optics in a solid-state waveguide, which is crucial for realizing quantum memories and sensing.
